attributes.title: Level 2

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you click the palette to select a background image for this project?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is it helpful to comment code? 

❓ Why do you think it’s especially helpful to use comments when coding in JavaScript?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to think about when they may have seen or used comments when coding in blocks. In the blocks editor, comments appear on a “sticky note” connected to a certain piece of code. In the JavaScript editor, comments are manually typed, using // to indicate a comment. They make it easier to organize code and identify specific parts of a program.

💡 Remind the ninja that they can click the right arrow, to the right of the line number, to minimize the code for an image.

💡 Walk the Ninja through how to drag out code from the menu to the right of the code comment, so that it appears on a new line. Alternatively, a blank line can be created and then the code block can be dragged directly there.
steps.instructions:
Set the greeting card theme by adding a background image to this project. 


Notice the code comment // set up on line 1 of the editor. In JavaScript, // signals a code comment and the slashes and text will appear in green. This text will be skipped over when the project is run.


Open Scene, drag [set background image to (img)] under the comment // set up, on line 2 of the editor.  

Click the palette to the left of the line of code to choose a festive background image from the Gallery.


Click ▶ to see the background image appear on screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type the sprite’s name in mySprite.setPosition(x, y), and update the x and y parameters?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why do you format a sprite’s name in camelCase?

❓ Which argument moves the sprite left and right on the screen? Which argument moves the sprite up and down on the screen? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that when using camelCase, spaces are replaced with capital letters.

💡 Help the ninja notice that after they’ve defined a sprite, when they begin retyping its name in another line of code, a pop up box will appear with the sprite’s name. The ninja can click on the sprite’s name and it will appear in the code, so that they do not need to type out the whole thing.

💡 As needed, the ninja can toggle back to blocks to use the visual coordinate grid to help them place a sprite in their desired location.
steps.instructions:
Add a sprite to this project and set its position! 


Open Sprites, drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] underneath the comment // sprite code then click the palette to select a sprite. Replace mySprite by typing a new sprite name using camelCase. Give the sprite a simple name that describes what it is, such as holidaySprite.


Open Sprites, drag [set (mySprite) position to x y] on a blank line under the existing code. Replace mySprite with the sprite’s name. Inside the parentheses, replace the first argument (0) with a number between 0 and 160 for the x position, and replace the second argument (0) with a number between 0 and 120 for the y position. 


Click ▶ to see the sprite appear on the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type the sprite’s name and update the different parameters inside the parentheses in mySprite.sayText(text, timeOnScreen, animated, textColor, textBoxColor)?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ When coding in blocks, were you able to change the color of the text or text box when a sprite said something?

❓ What symbol should be placed between each of the parameters, so that the code is able to run correctly?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Make sure the ninja does not include parentheses ( ) in the string parameter of the sayText function. This will prevent the validation from checking for the remaining parameters.

💡 Walk the ninja through the list of potential parameters and each argument’s type, using the documentation box as a guide. Remind the ninja that parameters need to be separated by commas , and strings should appear within quotation marks. The timeOnScreen number parameter represents the value in milliseconds. The animated Boolean parameter should have either true or false passed as its argument.

💡Explain to the ninja that JavaScript allows more customization options (particularly for the sayText function) than are available in blocks. In blocks, only the first three parameters are available. In JavaScript, the ninja is also able to customize the text and text box color.
steps.instructions:
Make the sprite say something in the greeting card! 


Open Sprites, drag [(this) say (:))] underneath the existing code. In the editor, highlight mySprite and replace it with the sprite’s name. Highlight the argument  :) inside the quotation marks, and replace the text with something for the sprite to say, such as “Happy Birthday!” 


After the closing quotation mark, type a comma , and notice the documentation box pop up: 



The sayText function has 5 possible parameters: text, timeOnScreen, animated, textColor, textBoxColor. Inside the parentheses, fill in the other 4 parameters with number or Boolean arguments, separated by commas, to customize the speech bubble. Use the documentation box for help with each parameter. 


Click ▶ to see the sprite say something in a customized speech bubble!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the parameter in pause(ms) to customize how long the project pauses?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What number is used as the timeOnScreen argument in the sayText function?

❓ Why should the pause argument be greater than or equal to the timeOnScreen argument?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 In the next step, a screen effect will be added to signal the ending celebration. Point out to the ninja that without adding a time delay, the screen effect would begin while the text is still on the screen. Help the ninja understand that the effect should happen after the text disappears from the screen.
steps.instructions:
Add a time delay so users can read the speech bubble before the celebration begins!


Open Loops, drag [pause (100) ms] underneath the existing code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

pause(100)

The pause function takes 1 parameter: the number of milliseconds to pause the program for. Inside the parentheses, replace the default argument (100) with a number equal to or larger than the timeOnScreen argument from the sayText function.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you choose an effect and update the parameters in effects.blizzard.startScreenEffect(duration, particlesPerSecond)?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What do you notice about the list of properties in the code completion tool? Do the effect names look familiar?

❓ What type of arguments should be placed inside the parentheses to set the duration and particlesPerSecond of the effect?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 If a ninja gets stuck, remind them that the dot operator . needs to be added after effects and before the effect name. This impacts the syntax and affects how the program finds the correct effect to run.

💡 Help the ninja notice the documentation box that pops up to check the syntax of the parameters. Point out to the ninja that both duration and particlesPerSecond take number arguments (in ms). This sets how long the effect appears, and how many pieces will appear on the screen per second. Prompt the Ninja to tinker with the values that set how long the effect will  appear on screen and what the volume of the effect is.
steps.instructions:
Add a celebration to the greeting card with a screen effect.


Open Scene, drag [start screen (effect) effect] underneath the existing code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

effects.blizzard.startScreenEffect()

Change the effect by highlighting .blizzard and deleting the text. Type . after effects to open the code completion tool of possible effects. Scroll down the list to the properties then select one that fits the theme of the greeting card.  


The startScreenEffect function takes 2 parameters: duration and particlesPerSecond. Inside the parentheses, fill in the 2 parameters with number arguments, separated by commas, to customize the screen effect. Use the documentation box for help with each parameter.


Click ▶ to see the screen effect appear on screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select a sound for your greeting card in music.melodyPlayable(music.Melody)?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What do you notice about the list of properties in the code completion tool? Do the sound names look familiar?

❓ What type of sound might fit the background image, sprite message, and screen effect of the greeting card?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that all of the same sounds are available for use in JavaScript that were available in blocks. The dot operator . opens the code completion tool and serves as the “drop down menu” that appears in blocks, and allows the ninja to add different sounds and effects to the project.
steps.instructions:
Add a fun sound to make the greeting card feel more celebratory!


Open Music, drag [play (to play) (playbackMode)] underneath the existing code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

music.play
(music.melodyPlayable(music.baDing), 
music.PlaybackMode.UntilDone)

Change the effect by highlighting .baDing and deleting the text. Type . after music to open the code completion tool list of possible sounds.


Scroll down the list to the properties then select one that fits the theme of the greeting card, like powerUp.


Click ▶ to hear the sound in the project!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you switch back to the blocks editor? What looks similar and what looks different?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Does the code work as expected in blocks?

❓ What is something new that you can do in JavaScript, that you weren’t able to do when coding in blocks?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Help the ninja make connections between the JavaScript text they have just written and their knowledge of blocks. Ninjas should be very familiar with these concepts already, so encourage them to think about the similarities and differences between blocks and text.
steps.instructions:
Test out the project. Does it work as expected?


Switch to the blocks editor to see what the JavaScript code looks like in blocks! Notice what is similar about the code, and what looks different: how are sprite names and other parameters formatted in blocks, compared to JavaScript?


Notice how the startScreenEffect and sayText functions turned into gray blocks. This is because they both have special parameters that are not available in the blocks editor. This is just one example of how coding in JavaScript will provide more opportunities to customize code.

subgroups.introduction: Create a greeting card project in JavaScript that uses properties to create music and screen effects!

validationItems.text: Use 1 sprite with a custom name and set its position.
Use the sayText function with 5 parameters.
Use a screen effect with 2 parameters.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 2 of Blue Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about properties and code comments. In JavaScript, you can type directly on the editor to organize your code using code comments and set different sprite properties. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 2:

badges.title: Parameter Pilot
badges.description: Use the JavaScript editor’s documentation and code completion tools when adding parameters to functions.

badges.title: Comment, Like, and Subscribe
badges.description: Add a comment to your code.

badges.title: Say What Now?
badges.description: Use the sayText function with all 5 parameters.

badges.title: Stop and Smell the Roses
badges.description: Use the pause function to temporarily stop your project from running new code.

badges.title: Effective Immediately
badges.description: Use the startScreenEffect function with 2 parameters.

badges.title: Music to My Ears
badges.description: Use the play function to play a melody.

badges.title: To Whom it May Concern
badges.description: Use the splash function to display a message on screen.

badges.title: A Speedy Recovery
badges.description: Set a sprite’s velocity property without using the setVelocity function.

badges.title: Wall of Text
badges.description: Use the showLongText function with 2 parameters.
